title: Privacy by Design
summary: Privacy by design is the principle that protection of personal data is built into a system, a process or a product from the beginning rather than added after it is finished. The idea was formulated by Ann Cavoukian and later taken into data protection law, most visibly in Article 25 of the General Data Protection Regulation, which requires data protection by design and by default. In practice it constrains engineering decisions at the point where they are cheap to change: what data is collected at all, why it is needed, how long it is kept, who can see it, and how it is deleted. The recognised techniques are familiar engineering ones used for a privacy goal, including data minimisation, purpose limitation, pseudonymisation, encryption, access control, retention limits and privacy protective defaults that apply without the user having to change a setting. The typical mistake is treating privacy by design as a legal sign off at the end of a project, at which point the only remaining options are paperwork or expensive rework. A second common gap is production reality: test data copied from live systems, debug logs, analytics events and backups are where personal data most often leaks, and they are rarely in the original design review.

exercises.summary: Recall and recognition: definitions, one clear answer, single-step questions.

exercises.title: Privacy by Design - EXTREMELY HARD

beginner.definition: Privacy by design means thinking about personal data protection before you build something. Personal data is any information that can identify a person, such as a name, phone number or address. You decide early what you really need to collect. Then you build the system so that less data is exposed and deleted when it is no longer needed.
beginner.whyItMatters: Data that was never collected cannot be lost in a breach. Fixing a design later costs far more than changing it at the start. Many countries also have laws that require this approach, with fines for careless handling. It also builds trust, because users notice when a service asks for less than it needs.
howItWorks: List the personal data the system will touch, including hidden copies in logs and backups.
Ask why each item is needed, and remove anything you cannot justify with a clear purpose.
Choose protective defaults so the safest setting applies without the user doing anything.
Limit who can see the data and use methods such as pseudonymisation to reduce exposure.
Set a retention period and build the deletion process before the data starts arriving.
Review the design again when the product changes, and check what production actually stores.
beginner.example: Imagine a library that issues membership cards. The librarian designs the form to ask for a name and a contact number only. She leaves out the birthday and the job title. The card number is stored instead of the name on the borrowing records. Old records are shredded after two years as a rule. If the record cabinet were ever opened by a stranger, most borrowers would stay unknown.
takeaways: Decide what data you need before you collect any of it.
Safe settings should be the default, not an option users must find.
Logs, test copies and backups hold personal data too, so include them in the design.

objectives: Explain what privacy by design means and why timing matters more than tooling.
Describe principles such as data minimisation, purpose limitation and protective defaults.
Give examples of privacy protective techniques such as pseudonymisation and retention limits.
Explain why data that is never collected carries no breach risk.
Identify places where personal data appears outside the main application, such as logs and backups.
Describe what a design review for personal data should ask before build work begins.
